The 18th century was the beginnings of the industrial revolution. It was a world
of coal and steam with noisy, smoky factories and long, hazardous labor. Within
a few generations it had transformed the way most people worked and the places
most people lived.

Much less conspicuously, the 18th century was also the beginnings of the modern,
global scientific enterprise. It witnessed the growth of scientific journals,
scientific meetings and scientific societies. Such communication and
collaboration became key elements in accelerating the pace of discovery in
science.

One of the greatest achievements of the 18th century scientists was the
discovery of electric charge.\* These researchers - through transatlantic
cooperation and transatlantic competition - modestly added charge to space and
time as a fundamental dimension of the natural world. Our modern lifestyles of
comfort and convenience are built on harnessing this dimension of nature.
Nowadays, the world of coal and steam seems ugly and unforgiving in comparison
to modern technology.

As humans we're mesmerized by lightning. Our ancient ancestors often attributed
lightning to supernatural forces. For example, the Greeks saw lightning as the
wrath of the God Zeus. For Nordic ancients it was Thor and for India ancients it
was Indra. But ultimately, it was 18th century scientists who - through creation
of artificial lighting in laboratory settings - were able to understand that
electric charge not angry Gods was actually responsible for lightning bolts.

Leyden jars were essential to experimental work on artificial lightning.
Although less dramatic than lightning in nature, these 'bottled' versions of
nature's strength could still provide a serious shock if mishandled.

Leyden jars were independently invented by a German clergyman and a Dutch
professor. The devices are essentially a glass container with a metal foil on
the inner surface and another metal foil on the outer surface. The jars were
developed to harvest the 'electricity' that's generated by friction. The sparks
of 'electric fire' were then released by connecting the two foils with a wire.
Both scientists documented receiving serious shocks.

Nowadays, we understand these jars as devices for collecting, storing and
releasing charge. The charge that's collected is charge that's 'harvested' by
rubbing, i.e., friction. The charge that's released is the cause of the spark,
i.e., lightning. Note the process of charging is a gradual collection while the
process of discharging is a instantaneous release. The is the powerful flash of
the lightning bolt.

To understand the workings of Leyden jars we've got to examine some properties
of conductors, e.g. metals. At microscopic levels, a metal is a vast sea of
fast-moving, negatively-charged electrons in an equally-vast array of fixed,
positively-charged ions. But at macroscopic levels, a metal is an electrical
landscape with zero electric field and constant electric potential.

Why? If the metal interior wasn't a zero-field landscape its electrons would
flow. This flow would continue until the metal becomes a zero-field landscape.
Essential the electrons can't \`rest' until the equilibrium of zero field is
reached. This cancellation is inevitable - the electrons can't \`rest' until the
electrical equilibrium of zero field and constant potential is reached.

Imagine placing a charge Q in the vicinity of a metal. The presence of charge Q
will cause the metal's electrons to move. This movement will continue until
throughout the metal, the evolving electric field of the metal, and fixed
electric field of the charge Q, cancel out. This cancellation is inevitable -
the electrons can't \`rest' until the electrical equilibrium of zero field and
constant potential is reached.

Similar things happen in charging a metal. Following the addition or removal of
charge, the metal's electrons will move and equilibrate the metal to zero field
and constant potential. Note the resulting regions of net charge of the charged
metal are always located on the metal's surface. This permits the electric
fields of these surface charges to be effectively \`expelled' into the
surrounding space.

Let's return to charging a Leyden jar. Typically, one deposits some charge, say
+Q, on the inner metal foil which induces an opposite charge, i.e., -Q, on the
outer metal foil. The outcome is equivalent to transferring a charge +Q from the
originally neutral, outer foil to the originally neutral, inner foil.

Note the charge +Q is located somewhere on the inner foil's surface and the
charge -Q is located somewhere on the outer foil's surface. The locations are
those that lead to zero field and constant potential in both foils.

If a wire connected to the inner foil and a wire connected to the outer foil are
brought into contact we get a spark. This spark is caused by the discharging of
the charges on the foils of the Leyden jar. This spark is what fascinated the
18th century scientists.

Nowadays we call a Leyden jar an electrical capacitor. A capacitor comprises a
pair of conducting plates separated by insulating material. For example, the
interior metal foil, the exterior metal foil, and the glass walls of the Leyden
jar.

There's a hurdle in understand capacitors. We don't know the locations of the
charges on the capacitor's plates. So, we can't directly figure the electric
field between the plates of a capacitor. And, we can't directly figure the
electric forces between the plates on a capacitor.

We'll use the concepts of electrical potential and electrical energy to
understand capacitors. On transferring charge Q between the plates a potential
difference ΔV appears between the plates. In charging the plates, you're raising
the potential of the positive plate and lowering the potential of the negative
plate. Increasing Q, increases ΔV.

It's analogous to digging a hole in the ground. Each shovel of earth is raising
some mass from lower to higher potential gravitational energy. Each shovel full
increases the potential of the bottom of the hole and the top of the pile.

What determines the proportionality between stored charge Q and potential
difference ΔV? It's the geometry and the material of the capacitor. The ratio of
Q to V is called the capacitance and all sorts of capacitors with all sorts of
capacitance are used in devices from washing machines to mobile phones.
Capacitors are devices for storing both charge and energy.

A special geometry of capacitors is the parallel plate capacitor. It comprises
two equal-area plates of area A and separation d. Its capacitance is C =
$\epsilon$A/d. Large area plates will yield a large capacitance and narrowly
separated plates will yield a large capacitance. The large area plates helps the
like charges on each plate spread out which makes the storing of charge cost
less energy. The small plate separations helps the opposite charges on opposite
plates get closer which makes the storing of charge easier.

Capacitors can be wired together. One way to wire-up two capacitors is in
parallel. If you connect two capacitors (C~1~, C~2~) in parallel you could walk
through the circuit by either passing through C~1~ or passing through C~2~.
Another way to wire-up two capacitors is in series. If you connect two
capacitors (C~1~, C~2~) in series you pass through C~1~ and pass through C~2~ to
walk through the circuit. Parallel is "\| \|" and series is "\_ \_". In
parallel, both capacitors have the same potential across their plates, but share
the stored charge. In series, both capacitors have the same charge on their
plates, but share the applied potential.

A very useful concept in solving problems of how the stored charge and applied
voltage are distributed over the capacitors in a capacitor circuit is the
equivalent capacitance. The equivalent capacitance of a capacitor circuit is the
single capacitor that stores the same charge and stores the same energy for the
same applied voltage. It's useful as once you know the equivalent capacitance of
a capacitor circuit its easy to figure the total charge stored by the circuit
for a given applied potential by C= Q/V. Knowing both the applied voltage and
stored charge, then allows the calculation of the sharing of the applied voltage
and the sharing of the stored charge over the circuit components.

The parallel arrangement is a circuit with a larger 'equivalent' capacitance, C
= C~1~ + C~2~ , and the series arrangement is a circuit with a smaller
'equivalent' capacitance, C^-1^ = C~1~^-1^ + C~2~^-1^ (equivalent capacitor
stores the same charge for the same potential). More complex circuits can
sometimes (not always) be dismantled into parallel and series parts to
understand the sharing of potentials and charges across individual capacitors.

\*The discovery was an early example of transatlantic cooperation between
researchers that forbears today's thousand-member, scientific collaborations
who've realized such discoveries as gravity waves, Higg's particles, and much
more.
